\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Standard confusion-matrix correction can reverse causal conclusions when misclassification rates vary across subgroups.
We derived an exact bias identity ($R^2 \geq 0.97$) that yields a diagnostic for flagging harmful correction and prescribes per-subgroup correction when $\Delta\pi > 0.15$ and $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, validated across 11 LLM--dataset combinations spanning eight LLMs and four NLP tasks.
For practitioners, we recommend a three-step protocol: (1)~estimate per-subgroup error rates from a pilot sample; (2)~apply the diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) to identify subgroups where global correction would increase bias; (3)~if $\Delta\pi > 0.15$ and the expert budget exceeds 250 labels, apply per-subgroup correction via EC-HTE.
When these conditions are not met, global correction remains appropriate; the diagnostic explicitly guards against inappropriate application.
The framework is task-agnostic and composes with prediction-powered inference~\cite{sui2026ppci}.

A key implication is that aggregate annotation accuracy---the metric most commonly reported in LLM annotation studies---is insufficient for downstream causal validity.
Two annotators with identical overall accuracy can produce qualitatively different causal conclusions if their error distributions across subgroups differ, as our CivilComments case study demonstrates (3.2$\times$ effect-size gap between identity subgroups masked by global correction).
The bias identity formalizes this insight: the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure shows that harm concentrates precisely where it is hardest to detect---in subgroups whose low error rates make them appear least problematic.

More broadly, as LLM annotation becomes standard practice in computational social science, the gap between average accuracy and subgroup-level reliability will grow with the diversity of populations studied.
Our bias identity provides a principled lens for auditing any pipeline that feeds machine-generated labels into downstream causal analysis.
We release an open-source implementation of the full EC-HTE pipeline, including the diagnostic, hierarchical Bayes estimation, and downstream CausalForest integration, to facilitate adoption.
Future directions include extending the framework to continuous covariates, scaling to larger $K$ via regularized estimation, and developing joint covariate--outcome correction methods that handle correlated misclassification across both the effect modifier and the response variable.

\section*{Ethical Considerations}

This work addresses bias in LLM-annotated causal inference, where misclassification rates can vary across demographic and text-feature subgroups.
Our CivilComments case study involves hate speech annotations stratified by identity subgroups (race, gender, religion); we use only the publicly released dataset~\cite{borkan2019nuanced} with no additional data collection or human annotation.
A central finding is that standard correction methods can mask or amplify disparities across subgroups---practitioners applying global debiasing without subgroup-level auditing risk drawing incorrect causal conclusions that disproportionately affect underrepresented populations.
We emphasize that EC-HTE is a diagnostic and correction tool, not a substitute for careful study design; subgroup definitions should be chosen based on domain knowledge and ethical considerations, not solely to optimize statistical metrics.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Measurement Error in Causal Inference}

Classical measurement error theory shows that naive regression with mismeasured covariates yields attenuated coefficients~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}.
\citet{frazis2003estimating} derive exact bias formulas for OLS with a misclassified binary regressor, showing attenuation proportional to the error rate---but restricted to average effects without subgroup heterogeneity.
In the econometrics literature, \citet{black2000racial} demonstrate that racial misclassification in administrative data biases disparity estimates, and \citet{bound2001measurement} survey how binary misclassification attenuates regression coefficients.
Our Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} generalizes the Frazis--Loewenstein scalar result to subgroup-heterogeneous error rates, revealing a qualitatively new product-form bias that can reverse effect signs across subgroups.

\subsection{Post-Prediction Causal Inference}

Several frameworks correct for machine-generated label noise in causal estimation.
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} and DSL~\cite{egami2023dsl} use a small expert-labeled sample to debias predictions, assuming homogeneous prediction quality across observations.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} extends this to outcome-side misclassification, and ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} uses forest-based instrumental variables.
\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark these methods, finding that debiasing can increase MSE when prediction error is heterogeneous---a population-level analogue of the subgroup-conditional bias amplification we formalize.
All assume a single global error model; none addresses per-subgroup effect modifier misclassification.

\subsection{Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}

Modern HTE estimators---causal forests~\cite{wager2018causal}, DML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml}, and recursive partitioning~\cite{athey2016recursive}---assume error-free covariates.
When the effect modifier $Z$ is an LLM annotation, error rates can vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups~\cite{ashwin2025bias}, violating this assumption.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification (errors in $T$, not $Z$), requiring instrumental variables; our setting preserves the treatment contrast but corrupts the heterogeneity structure, making confusion matrix inversion feasible.
Extended discussion appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.

**Abstract (plain text, no LaTeX):**
Large language models increasingly replace human annotators in computational social science, yet their error rates can vary by up to 5x across demographic and text-feature subgroups. When these noisy labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard remedy, estimating a single confusion matrix and applying its inverse uniformly, is widely trusted to remove bias.
